## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-level reasoning across 128-bit boundaries without loops or conditionals. Evaluates clean use of bitwise operations across data word boundaries and edge-case handling.

## Key Concepts
- 128-bit composition as two 64-bit halves
- Bitwise AND for intersection detection
- Bitwise OR to combine half-results
- Zero-check inference for disjointness

## Code Example
```c
int isDisjoint128(uint64_t hi1, uint64_t lo1, uint64_t hi2, uint64_t lo2) {
  uint64_t m = (hi1 & hi2) | (lo1 & lo2);
  return (m == 0) ? 1 : 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this to 256-bit masks?
- What's the performance impact on different architectures?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of cross-lane bit manipulation and wrap-around across a 128-bit value.

## Key Concepts
- 128-bit split across two uint64 halves
- Cross-lane bit movement with shifts
- Non-branching bitwise updates

```c
uint128 rotateLeft128_1(uint128 x) {
  uint64_t new_lo = (x.lo << 1) | (x.hi >> 63);
  uint64_t new_hi = (x.hi << 1) | (x.lo >> 63);
  uint128 r; r.hi = new_hi; r.lo = new_lo; return r;
}
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests a crisp bit-twiddling trick: constructing a mask anchored to the least significant set bit, plus proper zero handling.

## Key Concepts
- Isolating the LSB with n & -n
- Mask construction via (lsb<<1) - 1
- Edge-case handling for zero input

```javascript
function maskBelowLSB32(n) {

  return n === 0 ? 0 : (lsb << 1) - 1;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- What are the potential pitfalls on platforms with different integer sizes?

## Why This Is Asked
Tracks cross-word parity using SWAR folding without branches.

- Multi-word parity with bitwise folding
- SWAR technique to reduce 64-bit to 1 bit
- No loops or branches across 256 bits

```javascript
unsigned parity256(uint64_t a,uint64_t b,uint64_t c,uint64_t d){

```

questions.explanation:
This question tests bit manipulation without loops. Mask `0x55555555` (=0101... in binary) extracts even-position bits (0, 2, 4, ...), while `0xAAAAAAAA` (=1010... in binary) extracts odd-position bits (1, 3, 5, ...). The compression uses a parallel prefix technique: each stage combines adjacent bits via `(x | (x >> 1))`, then masks to keep only relevant pairs. Four repetitions shrink 32 bits down to 16. The odd bits are shifted right by 8 at the end to position them in the upper 16 bits.

Follow-up: For 64-bit input, repeat the algorithm on each 32-bit half, then combine the results.

## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to manipulate a 128-bit value using two 64-bit parts and leverage available intrinsics for performance. It tests understanding of bit significance ordering and boundary cases (zero input).

## Key Concepts

- 128-bit represented as two 64-bit words (lo then hi) and how trailing zeros map across the boundary
- Using 64-bit ctz intrinsics to build a 128-bit result in constant time
- Correct handling of the all-zero input returning 128

## Code Example

```c
int trailingZeroCount128(uint128 x) {
  if (x.lo != 0) return __builtin_ctzll(x.lo);
  if (x.hi != 0) return 64 + __builtin_ctzll(x.hi);
  return 128;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you implement this without compiler intrinsics?
- How would you port the approach to a 256-bit representation?
